records.title: $TagPlugin
records.text: The $TagPlugin powers the tags feature of Mosaic. This plugin scrapes $tag from page metadata and also applies all aliases stored in config.data.tags . Tags ultimately resolve down into refs , but are different from normal refs, in that they are applied to the union filesystem (all merged filesystems), not to the individual source filesystem that they were defined on. This can be thought of as a global ref . Other plugins can use config.setData() and modify the tags property, to apply new global refs, as long as they do so before this plugin has reaches $beforeSend .

records.title: $TagPlugin
records.text: This plugin runs with no special priority but it must run before both the $AliasPlugin and the $RefPlugin .

records.title: $TagPlugin
records.text: Let's assume there is a products page on your site and each product is shown as a tile. The information for each product tile is sourced from multiple Mosaic sources. How can tags be used to reference the product data needed for each tile on the products page? The product page should add a $tag metadata prop to its frontmatter: The tag shown in the example above is saying populate data.items of the Products index page with the data metadata property of pages tagged with product . A tagged product page needs to have a tags property which is a collection of tags and one of these needs to be product . This will allow the $TagPlugin to correctly associate the product page to the product index page. It will also need a data property because thats the property our product index page wants to use for the tiles.

records.title: TableOfContentsPlugin
records.text: The TableOfContentsPlugin generates a Table of Contents for each page in the Mosaic filesystem using the headings on the page. Heading ranks are used to determine which page headings should be included in the Table of Contents: | Heading Element (markdown syntax) | Rank | | --------------------------------- | ---- | | h1 (#) | 1 | | h2 (##) | 2 | | h3 (###) | 3 | | h4 (####) | 4 | | h5 (#####) | 5 | | h6 (######) | 6 | The plugin output is added to a tableOfContents metadata property of a page. Headings can include {meta.<path>} tokens, such as ## Examples for {meta.title} . The plugin replaces each token with the page's value, including values that come from a $ref . A token that doesn't resolve to text stays as it is, so you can spot it in the Table of Contents.

records.title: Write a plugin
records.text: A plugin changes pages as Mosaic loads them, from any source. Use one to add data to pages, fill in frontmatter, or write files for the whole site, such as an index. Mosaic's own default plugins are written the same way. A plugin can't change how pages look. Layouts and components belong to your site's code, and each page picks its layout with layout in its frontmatter.

records.title: Write a plugin
records.text: A plugin is a module whose default export holds one or more lifecycle methods . This one gives every page under a route the same layout, unless the page sets its own: Each lifecycle method gets its input (here, the source's pages), helpers such as the serialiser and namespace , and the options from the plugin's config. A page's frontmatter fields are properties of the page, and anything the plugin sets on a page is written to its frontmatter.

records.title: Write a plugin
records.text: Plugins are loaded with require.resolve , from inside Mosaic. Give the plugin's absolute path, or the name of an installed package: A plugin definition takes the same properties as a built-in plugin, such as priority and previewDisabled . See Configuration .

records.title: Write a plugin
records.text: Choose the earliest method that has what your plugin needs: | Method | Runs | Use it to | | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | $afterSource | In the source's worker, each time the source emits pages | Read or change pages one at a time. | | $beforeSend | In the source's worker | Read or write files across one source, and pass data to later methods with config.setData() . | | afterUpdate | In the main process | Read pages from every source with globalFilesystem , or write files for the whole site to sharedFilesystem , such as a sitemap. | | shouldClearCache | In the main process | Say whether another source's change affects this source's pages. | | shouldUpdateNamespaceSources | In the main process | Ask the other sources in a namespace to run afterNamespaceSourceUpdate . | Methods starting with $ run in each source's worker thread, so they can take time without holding up the server. The others run in the main process, so keep them fast. Plugins run each lifecycle method in order of priority , highest first. $ref s are not resolved yet in $afterSource . The $RefPlugin resolves them in $beforeSend , at priority -1 , so a plugin that reads values from $ref s should use $beforeSend with a lower priority, such as -1.5 .

records.title: Write a plugin
records.text: A failing plugin doesn't stop Mosaic: the error is recorded and the other plugins run. See Plugin errors . To name the page that caused an error, throw a PluginError with its path: In $afterSource , catch errors for each page and throw once after the loop, so one bad page doesn't stop the plugin for the pages after it.

records.title: Write a plugin
records.text: Lifecycle methods are plain functions, so test them by calling them: Then run mosaic build with your config and check the pages it writes.

We recommend storing a personal access token in an environment variable and using the environment variable in the source definition. This keeps credentials out of code where they may be accidentally exposed to third parties.

records.title: Git Repo Source
records.text: Set the save workflow's commitMessage option on each source to choose its default. Both GitHubPullRequestWorkflow and BitbucketPullRequestWorkflow accept a string or a callback: The callback runs on the server. Its first argument remains the backing virtual filesystem path, so existing one-argument callbacks still work. The second argument contains action ( create , update or rename ) and, when supplied, targetRoute . The source selected for the page supplies the default; the browser cannot select a different source. New pages follow the same ownership rules as saving a new page. The reference editor shows this default in Commit message , where the author can enter a summary and optional body. Reset to default restores the current suggestion. A rename updates the suggestion until the author edits it. Author text survives a failed save and closing/reopening the dialog for the same document; it resets after a successful save or a document change. Editing only the message does not enable saving an otherwise unchanged page. The submitted message takes precedence over the source default. With neither configured nor submitted, the built-in messages are docs: update <filePath> , docs: create <filePath> and docs: rename <filePath> to <targetRoute> . These replace the old ticket-specific fallback. Configured and submitted text is never rewritten for create or rename operations. Messages must contain non-whitespace text, fit within 8 KiB of UTF-8, and contain no control characters other than line endings. CRLF is normalized to LF; other text is preserved, with Git adding a terminal newline when the message has none. Explicitly blank messages are errors, while omitting the override keeps the configured default. Both providers use the first nonempty message line, trimmed, as the pull request summary. A nonempty titlePrefix is prepended as <titlePrefix> - <summary> ; set it to '' to use the summary alone. Long pull request titles are shortened to fit provider limits, including the prefix. The full commit message is preserved. The default prefix remains Mosaic Docs . The commit receives the full message, including its body. The final squash message is controlled by repository settings and the reviewer. Custom editor hosts opt in by passing loadSaveDefaults to Editor and forwarding the optional commitMessage in their persist handler. Hosts without that loader retain their existing save flow and show no message control. A custom workflow can expose a side-effect-free prepare hook returning { supportsCommitMessage: true, commitMessage: '...' } ; it must also honor and validate submitted messages in its action. Without the hook, defaults report { supportsCommitMessage: false } and the editor uses the existing save flow.

records.title: Git Repo Source
records.text: A git repo source checks its repository for new commits every checkIntervalMins (30 minutes by default, see Schedules ). Bitbucket Data Center can tell the Mosaic CLI about a push instead, so merged changes appear within seconds.

records.title: Git Repo Source
records.text: Generate a secret, for example with openssl rand -hex 32 , and set it as MOSAIC_BITBUCKET_WEBHOOK_SECRET on the CLI process. Without it the endpoint doesn't exist ( 404 ). In Bitbucket, open the repository's Repository settings → Webhooks and create a webhook: URL: https://<your Mosaic CLI host>/_mosaic_/webhooks/bitbucket Secret: the value of MOSAIC_BITBUCKET_WEBHOOK_SECRET Events: Repository → Push Select Test connection . The CLI answers 200 . Bitbucket must be able to reach the CLI over HTTP(S), so open any firewall or proxy in between for this path. The endpoint doesn't use MOSAIC_ADMIN_SECRET : it only accepts requests signed with the webhook secret (the X-Hub-Signature header).

records.title: Git Repo Source
records.text: The CLI looks for running git repo sources whose options.repo is the pushed repository and whose options.branch was pushed. Repositories match on project key and repository slug, ignoring case and credentials, so the https://host/scm/PROJ/repo.git , ssh://git@host:7999/proj/repo.git and https://host/projects/PROJ/repos/repo forms all work. The CLI replies 202 straight away, with the names of the matching sources, and refreshes them in the background. Pushes that reach the same source within 5 seconds are combined into one refresh. A refresh does what a scheduled check does: it fetches, resets the clone to the new commit and re-reads the changed pages, while the source keeps serving its current pages. If MOSAIC_REVALIDATE_URL is set, the site is then told to revalidate as for any other update. | Response | When | | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | 200 | Bitbucket's Test connection ( diagnostics:ping ) | | 202 | A push was received; sources lists the sources being refreshed (it may be empty) | | 202 | Any other event; it is ignored | | 400 | The push payload isn't valid | | 401 | The X-Hub-Signature header is missing or doesn't match the body and the secret | | 404 | MOSAIC_BITBUCKET_WEBHOOK_SECRET isn't set | | 413 | The body is larger than 1 MB | To test the endpoint by hand, sign the body with the secret:

records.title: Git Repo Source
records.text: Polling stays on. A delivery the CLI misses (it was restarting, or the network dropped it) is picked up at the next scheduled check. With webhooks in place you can make that check less frequent, for example schedule: { checkIntervalMins: 240, initialDelayMs: 1000 } on the source (see Schedules ). Several CLI instances each check on their own schedule, but only the instance that receives the webhook refreshes straight away. If the webhook URL points at a load balancer, the other instances catch up at their next check; add a webhook per instance if they must all update at once. Snapshot and static deployments have no running CLI to call. Trigger a rebuild from your CI pipeline on push instead. Only Bitbucket Data Center push events are supported. Bitbucket Cloud and GitHub webhooks are not.

records.title: HTTP Source
records.text: The HTTP Source is used to pull content over HTTP. Multiple endpoints can be specified and the source will combine and transform the response from each into a single collection of pages.

records.title: HTTP Source
records.text: yarn add @jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-http

records.title: HTTP Source
records.text: | Property | Description | Required | | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | | modulePath | The path to the installed module (@jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-http) | Yes | | namespace | The scope for this source | Yes | | disabled | When true, content from this source is not used | No | | options.endpoints | Collection of URLS to make requests | Yes | | options.prefixDir | The root path used in the content URL | Yes | | options.transformResponseToPagesModulePath | The path of the module used to transform endpoint responses into Mosaic pages | Yes | | options.checkIntervalMins | Number of minutes to wait between requests. Defaults to 5 minutes | No | | options.initialDelayMs | Number of milliseconds to wait for making initial request. Defaults to 1000 | No | | options.requestTimeout | Milliseconds to wait for each response, including its body, before reporting an error. Defaults to 5000 | No |

records.title: Sources
records.text: Sources are what Mosaic uses to pull content from disparate locations and merge into a single virtual filesystem that can be used by a Mosaic Site. Depending on the mode used, sources can update periodically ensuring that new content is made available automatically.

records.title: Sources
records.text: Source Definitions are specified in the sources collection of a mosaic config file. Each source uses a zod schema to validate the provided JSON to ensure that all required information for the source to pull content has been provided. A source definition at a minimum needs to provide the module path of the source and the namespace that it will use. A namespace is not unique across sources though it is common that each source has a different namespace. Lastly, the options field can be used as a bucket for configuration values needed to configure the source e.g. credentials. Users are free to add any property as a source option but please read the gotchas first regarding the allowed values .

records.title: Sources
records.text: A Source Namespace is a scoping mechanism for Mosaic sources used to filter the content loaded by Mosaic. By default all sources specified in the mosaic config file are loaded. The following command will ensure mosaic only loads sources with the local scope.

records.title: Sources
records.text: Source schedules define how often sources pull in content that exists remotely and if a failed source is retried. More information can be found here

records.title: Sources
records.text: Out of the box, Mosaic provides 3 source "types": Local Folder Git Repo Source HTTP Source Sources must expose an observable interface so it is possible to compose sources together e.g. the Git Repo source uses the Local Folder source internally to watch the cloned folder for changes. To bring in content from somewhere else, write a source .

records.title: Sources
records.text: When running in active mode , Mosaic will watch for any changes to the source content and if a change is detected, will initiate a pull of that new content. How often to check for updates and how updates are triggered are a matter for the source to handle. Mosaic simply responds when a source emits new content.

records.title: Sources
records.text: Sources are executed inside their own worker thread to ensure that the main thread is not overloaded. It is here that a local virtual filesystem for the source is created and where several of the Plugin Lifecycle events are triggered.

records.title: Sources
records.text: A service worker thread uses postMessage to communicate with the main thread and vice-versa. This is important because it limits what values can be provided in the source definition to those that can be processed by the Structured Clone Algorithm .

records.title: Local Folder Source
records.text: The Local Folder Source is used to pull content from a folder located on the same machine as Mosaic is running. It is common to use this source when running mosaic locally.

records.title: Local Folder Source
records.text: yarn add @jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-local-folder

records.title: Local Folder Source
records.text: | Property | Description | Required | | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------- | | modulePath | The path to the installed module (@jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-local-folder) | Yes | | namespace | The scope for this source | Yes | | disabled | When true, content from this source is not used | No | | options.rootDir | The top level directory content will be pulled from | Yes | | options.prefixDir | The root path used in the content URL | Yes | | options.extensions | Collection of file extensions that the source will look for inside the rootDir | Yes |

records.title: Local Folder Source
records.text: This source will look for content with the ".mdx" extension in a "docs" directory 2 levels up from the Mosaic working directory. That content is included in the "local" namespace and available from a route that is prefixed with "local". So if you had a file, docs/app/index.mdx then you would be able to view it at http://localhost:3000/local/app/index .

records.title: Source Schedules
records.text: A source schedule defines how often a source initiates a content pull and what to do when there is a failure. A schedule can be specified for each source in the source definition, but should a source not provide a schedule it will inherit the "global" schedule. Git repo sources can also be refreshed as soon as Bitbucket reports a push, with the schedule as a fallback. See Refresh on push .

records.title: Source Schedules
records.text: | Property | Description | Required | Default | | ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | ------- | | checkIntervalMins | The length of time in minutes before triggering a content refresh | Yes | 30 mins | | initialDelayMs | Startup delay for the source. | Yes | 1000 ms | | retryEnabled | When true, failures will trigger another content pull | No | true | | retryDelayMins | The interval between retries. This will rise exponentially on every failure. | No | 5 | | maxRetries | Maximum number of retry attempts | No | 100 | | resetOnSuccess | If true, when a source recovers and emits pages it's retry counter is returned to zero | No | true |

records.title: Source Schedules
records.text: The global schedule applies to all sources that do not provide their own schedule. It can be configured as a top-level property of the Mosaic config file.

records.title: Source Schedules
records.text: Given the config file below: Source A will inherit the global schedule so it will: Start after a 1 second delay Pull content every 30 minutes Retry a failed content pull after an initial 5 minute delay Retry 10 times and if still unsuccessful, closing Source B has its own schedule so it will: Start after a 5 second delay Pull content every 60 minutes Retry a failed content pull after an initial 30 minute delay Retry 50 times and if still unsuccessful, closing

records.title: Source Schedules
records.text: The retry strategy that Mosaic employs is Exponential Backoff . This is a common strategy for networking applications that aims to prevent retries from causing more harm than good. For example, given a source schedule that has a 1 minute retry delay and will retry a maximum of 3 times then the total time spent retrying is 7 minutes: 1 minute delay then 1st retry 2 minute delay then 2nd retry 4 minute delay then 3rd (and final) retry Total delay: 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 minutes As you can see, the delay between retries is growing exponentially giving the content source more time to recover after each retry.

records.title: Figma Source
records.text: The Figma source is used to pull individual design patterns from Figma projects. The source subscribes to Figma project groups, then extracts from project files, tagged patterns. A Figma pattern tag is defined within a Figma project's sharedPluginData . For each retrieved/tagged pattern, a page is created in the Mosaic file-system. Additional Mosaic metadata can be added, to each created page, using meta For instance we could add metadata which defines which product owns a particular pattern and then group patterns based on owner.

records.title: Figma Source
records.text: yarn add @jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-figma

records.title: Figma Source
records.text: The Figma source is an HttpSource and shares the same base configuration. The transformResponseToPagesModulePath prop has a default transformer which creates a page for each matching Story. | Property | Description | Required | | ---------- | --------------------------------- | -------- | | prefixDir | path to store figma patterns | Yes | | figmaToken | figma access token | Yes | | projects | array of projects to subscribe to | Yes | | endpoints | figma endpoints | Yes | Each project is configured from the projects array. | Property | Description | Required | | ------------- | --------------------------------------------- | -------- | | id | numerical id of the subscribed project group | Yes | | meta | metadata to add to each of the projects pages | Yes | | patternPrefix | prefix to add to all pages created | Yes | endpoints defined the Figma REST API endpoints. | Property | Description | Required | | ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | | getProject | url to return a list of projects within the project group | Yes | | getFile | url to return a project file | Yes | | generateThumbnail | url to generate a thumbnail for the shared Figma node | Yes |

records.title: Readme Source
records.text: The Readme source is used to pull individual Readme.md text files from repositories. This is a lighter weight version of a Git repository resource, which just pulls a single file, rather the whole contents of the repo. For each retrieved readme, a page is created in the Mosaic file-system. Additional Mosaic metadata can be added, to each created page, using meta For instance we could add metadata which defines which product owns a particular Readme.md and then group this page, with others, based on owner.

records.title: Readme Source
records.text: yarn add @jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-readme

records.title: Readme Source
records.text: The Readme source is an HttpSource and shares the same base configuration. | Property | Description | Required | | ----------- | --------------------- | -------- | | accessToken | request access token | Yes | | prefixDir | path to store pages | Yes | | readme | array of readme files | Yes | Each readme is configured from the readme array. | Property | Description | Required | | --------------- | ---------------------------- | -------- | | contentTemplate | template for content of page | No | | name | page name used in route | Yes | | readmeUrl | url of readme | Yes | | meta | metadata for page | Yes |

records.title: Storybook Source
records.text: The Storybook source is used to pull individual stories from Storybook, based on tags. The Mosaic source will filter your Storybook's stories, based on title or tags . For each matching story, a page is created in the Mosaic file-system. additional Mosaic tags can be added to each page using additionalTags additional Mosaic metadata can be added to each page using additionalData This information can be used to create a dynamic index of stories from Storybook.

records.title: Storybook Source
records.text: yarn add @jpmorganchase/mosaic-source-storybook

records.title: Storybook Source
records.text: The Storybook source is an HttpSource and shares the same base configuration. The transformResponseToPagesModulePath prop has a default transformer which creates a page for each matching Story. The stories option is an array of Storybook urls that are used as Sources. Each story is matched on title using the filter Regexp (or by filterTags ). If specified, additionalTags and additionalData can be added to any matching pages. | Property | Description | Required | | --------------- | ---------------------- | -------- | | options.stories | array of story configs | Yes | stories is an array of Storybooks that you want to pull stories from | Property | Description | Required | | -------------- | ---------------------------------------- | -------- | | storyUrlPrefix | prefix url of the storybook deployment | Yes | | description | description of the storybook stories | Yes | | storiesUrl | url of the storybook's stories.json | No | | filter | RegExp filter to match on | No | | filterTags | Array of Storybook tags to match on | No | | meta | additional data to add to matching pages | No |

records.title: Write a source
records.text: A source brings pages into Mosaic. Before writing one, check whether a built-in source covers it: Files in a folder or a Git repository: use the Local Folder or Git Repo source. JSON from HTTP endpoints: use the HTTP Source with a transformer module, transformResponseToPagesModulePath . The transformer is a function that receives each response and returns pages, so you don't need a source of your own. Write a source when the content needs code to fetch, such as a system with its own client or authentication.

records.title: Write a source
records.text: A source is a module whose default export has a create function. create receives the source's options from your config and returns an RxJS observable of pages. This one emits a glossary page for each term from another system, then checks for changes on the source's schedule : Each page needs: fullPath : the page's file path, ending in one of the config's pageExtensions , such as .mdx . Mosaic leaves out pages without one, with a warning. route : the page's URL. Defaults to fullPath . Mosaic lowercases both. content : the page body, without frontmatter. Any other property, such as title , description or layout , becomes the page's frontmatter. Emit every page each time. Each emission replaces all of the source's pages, so a page that's left out of an emission is removed. create 's second argument also has the config's pageExtensions and a serialiser for those extensions, for sources that read files with frontmatter.

records.title: Write a source
records.text: Sources are loaded with import() , from inside Mosaic. Give the source's file URL, or the name of an installed package: Each source runs in its own worker thread, so its options must be values that can be copied between threads : no functions or class instances. See Source Definitions for the other properties, such as schedule .

records.title: Write a source
records.text: Alongside create , a source can export: refresh(options) : check for changes now rather than at the next scheduled check, for example when a webhook arrives. Emit any changed pages on the observable create returned. capabilities : what the source supports. { writable: true } lets editors change its pages in the content editor. Only set it when the source has a workflow that saves the changes, as the Git Repo source does with pull requests.

records.title: Write a source
records.text: Run mosaic build with your config, and check the pages it writes: To change pages from every source, rather than to add pages, write a plugin instead.

records.title: Custom Components
records.text: Learn how to add your own custom components to your Mosaic site.

records.title: Custom Components
records.text: An extension that renders Mosaic components or calls its hooks must use the host's React and Mosaic contexts. Declare the Mosaic packages it imports as peerDependencies , and add the same versions to devDependencies for local development. For example, an extension tested with the beta.98 release can declare: Externalize those peers when bundling the extension, including their subpath imports. Listing peers does not stop a bundler from embedding a second copy. A bundled or separately installed mosaic-store , for example, creates a different context: its hooks cannot see the host's StoreProvider or ColorModeProvider . The host installs the packages and chooses one Mosaic release cohort. Test the packed extension against the host's providers, including an interaction that updates shared state. See Trying a snapshot for preview versions.

records.title: Custom Components
records.text: To start, create a components folder under src where you'll store your custom components. In this tutorial, we will create a custom Card component.

records.title: Custom Components
records.text: Open your site's MDX component registry at src/app/[namespace]/[...route]/MdxComponents.ts . This file is the App Router equivalent of the old pages/_app.tsx component-merge step — the catch-all route imports the exported mdxComponents map and forwards it to <Body components={...} /> . Add the following line to your imports: Replace this block: with: This will add your custom components to the site, and any custom components in myComponents will override the corresponding ones in mosaicComponents . The spread operator ( ... ) merges both mosaicComponents and myComponents objects, giving priority to myComponents when there is a naming conflict. Note: MdxComponents.ts is marked 'use client' . Salt DS and any other component that uses hooks must be reachable from a client boundary. records.title: Custom CSS
records.text: You can customize the look and feel of your Mosaic site by creating cusotm CSS files. Here is a step-by-step guide to help you create your own CSS theme.

records.title: Custom CSS
records.text: To get started, create a folder named "css" in the "src" folder of your Mosaic project.

records.title: Custom CSS
records.text: Inside the "css" folder, create a folder named "global". This is where you will add your custom styles. Create an "index.css" file inside the "css" folder. This file will import your custom styles. Inside your global folder, create a separate CSS file for each part of your site that you want to customize. For instance, if you want to change the text styling, create a "text.css" file inside the "global" folder. Here is an example of how your "text.css" file could look like: You can add as many CSS files as you need, depending on how much you want to customize your site. Create an "index.css" file inside the "global" folder. This file will import your custom styles, in this example we are importing our "text.css" file. Your "css" folder should now look like this:

records.title: Custom CSS
headings: Import your custom CSS into your site
records.text: To apply your custom styles to your Mosaic site, open your src/app/layout.tsx file and add the following line to the bottom of your imports: Note: in the App Router, global CSS must be imported from the root layout ( app/layout.tsx ). Importing global CSS from a client component or any non-layout file is rejected by Next.js at build time. Congratulations! You have successfully applied your custom CSS styles to your site. This example demonstrated how to create text styles, but you can use the same approach to customize other aspects of your site as well.

records.title: $afterSource
records.text: The first lifecycle event to trigger after receiving pages from a source and runs in a child process. The pages can safely be mutated and will be reflected in the final filesystem that gets generated. It must return a collection of pages. The $afterSource lifecycle event is called with: pages - the collection of pages emitted by the source helpers - an object with useful methods options - the options specified for the plugin in the mosaic config file

records.title: $afterSource
records.text: The helpers provided with this lifecycle event are listed in the table below. | Property | Description | | -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | serialiser | A matching Serialiser for serialising/deserialising pages when reading/writing to the filesystem | | config | A mutable object for sharing data with other lifecycle phases of all plugins for this source (including in the main thread) in this plugin | | pageExtensions | A collection of pageExtensions the source is using | | ignorePages | A collection of page globs that are to be ignored for this source | | namespace | The namespace of the source running the plugin |

records.title: afterUpdate
records.text: The third lifecycle event to trigger overall and the first to trigger inside the main Mosaic process. Calls after the filesystem and symlinks have been reconstructed due to a change to the current source pages. Pages will not be cached when read at this stage, to allow for reading content and writing a new copy of it without the cached version taking effect. This method is safe to use with lazy loading, as the filesystem should return the full page when read. The afterUpdate lifecycle event is called with: mutableFilesystem - Mutable filesystem instance with all of this source's pages inside (and symlinks re-applied) helpers - an object with useful methods options - the options specified for the plugin in the mosaic config file

records.title: afterUpdate
records.text: The helpers provided with this lifecycle event are listed in the table below. | Property | Description | | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | serialiser | A matching Serialiser for serialising/deserialising pages when reading/writing to the filesystem | | config | An immutable object for reading data from other lifecycle phases of all plugins for this source in the child process for this plugin. Shared only with this source. | | globalConfig | An immutable object for reading data from other lifecycle phases of all plugins. Shared across all sources. | | sharedFilesystem | Mutable filesystem instance independent of any sources. Useful for global pages, like sitemaps | | globalFilesystem | Immutable union filesystem instance with all source's pages (and symlinks applied) | | pageExtensions | A collection of pageExtensions the source is using | | ignorePages | A collection of page globs that are to be ignored for this source | | namespace | The namespace of the source running the plugin |

records.title: $beforeSend
records.text: The second lifecycle event to trigger and does so after a filesystem has been built up from the source pages. It is the last lifecycle event to run in a source child process before the filesystem is sent to the main Mosaic process and should not return a value. The $beforeSend lifecycle event is called with: mutableFilesystem - Mutable virtual filesystem instance with all of this source's pages inside (and symlinks applied) helpers - an object with useful methods options - the options specified for the plugin in the mosaic config file

records.title: $beforeSend
records.text: The helpers provided with this lifecycle event are listed in the table below. | Property | Description | | -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | serialiser | A matching Serialiser for serialising/deserialising pages when reading/writing to the filesystem | | config | A mutable object for sharing data with other lifecycle phases of all plugins for this source (including in the main thread) in this plugin | | pageExtensions | A collection of pageExtensions the source is using | | ignorePages | A collection of page globs that are to be ignored for this source | | namespace | The namespace of the source running the plugin |

records.title: Lifecycle Events
records.text: The plugin lifecycle is triggered when a source emits content. Each Mosaic source has its own worker thread and plugin lifecycle events that start with a $ will execute inside the worker thread. All other lifecycle events will execute in the main Mosaic process. The 5 lifecycle events are: $afterSource $beforeSend afterUpdate shouldClearCache shouldUpdateNamespaceSources Plugin methods that trigger inside the main thread should be asynchronous and highly optimised to avoid holding up the main thread.

records.title: shouldClearCache
records.text: The fourth lifecycle event to trigger overall and the second to trigger inside the main Mosaic process. It is called every time any source emits new pages and should return a boolean to indicate if other sources should clear their cache in response to the source updating. Only sources that have already run afterUpdate will call this lifecycle hook since there is no cache to clear if they haven't reached that stage in the lifecycle. The shouldClearCache lifecycle event is called with: updatedSourceFilesystem - Immutable filesystem for the source that changed i.e, not the source filesystem helpers - an object with useful methods options - the options specified for the plugin in the mosaic config file

records.text: The helpers provided with this lifecycle event are listed in the table below. | Property | Description | | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | serialiser | A matching Serialiser for serialising/deserialising pages when reading/writing to the filesystem | | config | An immutable object for reading data from other lifecycle phases of all plugins for this source in the child process for this plugin. Shared only with this source. | | globalFilesystem | Immutable union filesystem instance with all source's pages (and symlinks applied) | | pageExtensions | A collection of pageExtensions the source is using | | ignorePages | A collection of page globs that are to be ignored for this source | | namespace | The namespace of the source running the plugin |

records.title: shouldUpdateNamespaceSources
records.text: The fifth lifecycle event to trigger overall and the third to trigger inside the main Mosaic process. It is called every time any source emits new pages and should return a boolean to indicate if other sources that share the same source namespace should re-run afterUpdate . The shouldUpdateNamespaceSources lifecycle event is called with: updatedSourceFilesystem - Immutable filesystem for the source that changed i.e, not the source filesystem helpers - an object with useful methods options - the options specified for the plugin in the mosaic config file
